topic: 3 real reasons honey never spoils, even after 3,000 years in an Egyptian tomb
title: 3 Real Reasons Honey Never Goes Bad (Even After 3,000 Years)
description: Archaeologists have pulled honey out of Egyptian tombs thousands of years old and it was still edible. This AI-narrated short breaks down the actual chemistry behind it -- no water for bacteria, high acidity, and a natural antiseptic bees make themselves -- not just the trivia everyone already knows.

hook_candidates.text: Archaeologists once dug up 3,000-year-old honey from an Egyptian tomb -- and ate it.
Honey survives 3,000 years in a tomb, for exactly 3 reasons.
Why is honey the one food that never actually goes bad?
That expiration date on your honey jar doesn't actually mean anything.

payoff_mechanism: Honey resists bacteria because it has almost no free water for microbes to use, it is acidic enough to block most bacterial growth, and bees' own glucose oxidase enzyme slowly produces hydrogen peroxide, a natural antiseptic, as the honey sits.

beats.text: Honey survives **3,000 years** in a tomb, for exactly 3 reasons.
One -- barely any **water**, so bacteria can't survive in it.
Two -- it's too **acidic** for bacteria to grow.
Three -- bees' own enzyme slowly turns into **hydrogen peroxide**, a natural antiseptic that keeps bacteria from growing.
Not magic -- just **chemistry** that outlasted the pyramids. Follow for the next one.
